transcription.tex: \textbf{From particles to rigid bodies}\par A particle model ignores an object’s dimensions. A rigid-body model includes its size and shape, so it can describe rotation.\par A rod is a thin rigid body. A lamina is a thin, flat body.\par A hanging bucket can be treated as a particle when only its weight and the supporting tension matter.

\textbf{Three ideas in this chapter}\par 1. Equilibrium: the resultant force and resultant moment are both zero.\par 2. Centre of mass: a uniform rod’s weight acts at its midpoint; a non-uniform rod’s need not.\par 3. Tilting: a support about to lose contact exerts no reaction. Use the remaining pivot to take moments.

transcription.tex: \textbf{Equilibrium of a rigid body}\par Both conditions are required:\[\sum\mathbf F=\mathbf0,\qquad\sum M=0.\]\par For vertical forces, total upward force equals total downward force. About any point, total clockwise moment equals total anticlockwise moment.

shapes.alt: Two people sit on a balanced seesaw, ten and eight metres from its pivot.

transcription.tex: \textbf{A reliable method}
1. Draw the external forces.
2. Place a uniform rod’s weight at its midpoint.
3. Resolve forces.
4. Take moments about a point that eliminates an unwanted force.
5. Check units and the physical meaning of the answer.

transcription.tex: Woody and Buzz are having fun on a uniform seesaw of mass 20 kg. Woody has mass 70 kg and is 10 m from the pivot. Buzz is 8 m from the pivot. The seesaw remains horizontal.\par (a) Determine the reaction force at the pivot of the seesaw.\par (b) Determine Buzz’s mass.

shapes.alt: Woody, the seesaw and Buzz exert downward weights. The pivot exerts an upward reaction.

transcription.tex: Take moments about \(B\), where Buzz sits. His unknown weight has zero moment about this point. The plank’s midpoint is 9 m from \(B\).\[8R=70g(18)+20g(9).\]Hence \(R=180g=1764\) N upwards.
Resolve vertically: \(R=(70+20+m)g\). Substituting \(R=180g\) gives \(m=180-90=90\) kg.
Alternatively, take moments about the pivot \(P\). The plank’s weight acts 1 m to its left.\[70g(10)+20g(1)=mg(8).\]This gives \(m=90\) kg. Then \(R=(70+20+90)g=1764\) N.

transcription.tex: A uniform beam \(AB\), of mass 40 kg and length 5m, rests horizontally on support at \(C\) and \(D\), where \(AC=DB=1\) m. When a man of mass 80kg stands on the beam at \(E\) the magnitude of the reaction at \(D\) is twice the magnitude of the reaction at \(C\).\par By modelling the beam as a rod and the man as a particle, find the distance \(AE\).

shapes.alt: Forces on the beam and man together, with AE marked as the unknown distance x.

transcription.tex: Let the reactions at \(C,D\) be \(R,2R\). Vertical equilibrium gives \(R+2R=(40+80)g\), so \(R=40g\).\par Put \(AE=x\). Taking moments about \(A\) gives \(40g(1)+80g(4)=40g(2.5)+80gx\).\par Divide by \(g\): \(360=100+80x\), hence \(AE=3.25\,\mathrm m\). The beam is a rod and the man is a particle, so his weight acts at \(E\).

transcription.tex: Question 9

A uniform beam \(AB\) has weight \(W\) N and length 8 m. The beam is held in a horizontal position in equilibrium by two vertical light inextensible wires attached to the beam at the points \(A\) and \(C\) where \(AC=4.5\) m, as shown in the diagram. A particle of weight 30 N is attached to the beam at \(B\).\par (a) Show that the tension in the wire attached to the beam at \(C\) is \(\left(\tfrac89 W+\tfrac{160}{3}\right)\mathrm N\).\par (b) Find, in terms of \(W\), the tension in the wire attached to the beam at \(A\).\par Given that the tension in the wire attached to the beam at \(C\) is twelve times the tension in the wire attached to the beam at \(A\),\par (c) find the value of \(W\).

shapes.alt: Eight-metre beam with wires at A and C, and a 30 newton particle at B.

transcription.tex: (a) Take moments about \(A\). The weight of the uniform beam acts at its midpoint, 4 m from \(A\).\[4.5T_C=4W+8(30).\]Hence \(T_C=(8W+480)/9=\tfrac89W+\tfrac{160}{3}\) newtons.
(b) Resolve vertically: \(T_A+T_C=W+30\). Substitution gives \(T_A=W+30-\tfrac89W-\tfrac{160}{3}=\tfrac19W-\tfrac{70}{3}\) newtons.
(c) Put \(T_C=12T_A\). Multiply by 9 to give \(8W+480=12(W-210)\). Hence \(4W=3000\) and \(W=750\). The tensions are 60 N and 720 N, as required.

A seesaw in a playground consists of a beam \(AB\) of length 10 m which is supported by a smooth pivot at its centre \(C\). Sophia has mass 30 kg and sits on the end \(A\). Roshan has mass 50 kg and sits at a distance \(x\) metres from \(C\), as shown in the diagram. The beam is initially modelled as a uniform rod. Using this model,\par (a) find the value of \(x\) for which the seesaw can rest in equilibrium in a horizontal position.\par (b) State what is implied by the modelling assumption that the beam is uniform.\par Roshan finds he must sit at a distance of 4 m from \(C\) for the seesaw to rest horizontally in equilibrium. The beam is now modelled as a non-uniform rod of mass 25 kg. Using this model,\par (c) find the distance of the centre of mass of the beam from \(C\).

shapes.alt: Sophia sits at A and Roshan a distance x to the right of the central pivot C.

transcription.tex: (a) The weight of the uniform beam acts at \(C\), so its moment there is zero. Take moments about \(C\): \(30g(5)=50gx\). Therefore \(x=3\).
(b) The mass is distributed uniformly along the beam, so the centre of mass is at its midpoint \(C\).

(c) Roshan now gives a clockwise moment of \(50g(4)=200g\), while Sophia gives \(150g\) anticlockwise. The beam must contribute the missing anticlockwise moment. Let its centre of mass lie \(d\) metres towards Sophia. Then \(30g(5)+25gd=50g(4)\), giving \(25d=50\). It is 2 m from \(C\), towards \(A\).
Question 7

A non-uniform rod AB, of length 25 m and weight 80 N, rests horizontally in equilibrium on supports C and D as shown in the diagram. The centre of mass of the rod is 10 m from A. A particle of weight W newtons is attached to the rod at a point E, where E is x metres from A. The rod remains in equilibrium and the magnitude of the reaction at C is five times the magnitude of the reaction at D. Show that $W=\frac{400}{25-3x}$

transcription.tex: Question 8

A non-uniform rod of weight 100 N and length 4 m is freely hinged to a vertical wall, and held in place by a cable attached at an angle of 30° to the end of the rod. Given that the tension in the cable is 80 N and that the rod is held in horizontal equilibrium, find the distance of the centre of mass of the rod from the wall.

shapes.alt: A wall cable pulls the free end of a four-metre horizontal rod up and towards the wall at 30 degrees.

transcription.tex: Moments about the hinge:\[100x=80(4\sin30^\circ)=160.\]\[x=1.6\text{ m}.\]

transcription.tex: Extension question

A non-uniform beam of weight 120 N and length 5 m is smoothly pivoted at a point M and is held at an angle of 40° by a cable attached at point N. Given that the tension in the cable is 30 N and it makes an angle of 80° with the beam, find the distance of the centre of mass of the beam from M.

shapes.alt: An inclined beam MN, hinged at M, with a cable pulling up-left on N at 80 degrees to NM.

transcription.tex: Let the centre of mass be \(x\) metres along the beam.\[120x\cos40^\circ=30(5\sin80^\circ).\]\[x=\frac{5\sin80^\circ}{4\cos40^\circ}=1.61\text{ m (3 s.f.)}.\]

transcription.tex: Woody gradually increases the weight he is applying at one end of a beam, until the rod is on the verge of tilting about the support \(A\). What can we say about the forces at \(B\)?

transcription.tex: The beam is just losing contact at \(B\), so \(R_B=0\). The reaction at \(A\) still supports the load.\par Use this threshold condition before taking moments about \(A\). In a suspended system, a cable which is just becoming slack likewise has zero tension.

transcription.tex: A uniform beam \(AB\), of mass 45kg and length 16m, rests horizontally on supports \(C\) and \(D\) where \(AC=5\) m and \(CD=9\) m.\par When Woody stands at \(A\), the beam is on the point of tilting about \(C\).\par Determine Woody’s mass.

shapes.alt: The load acts at A. The uniform beam weight acts at G, three metres right of pivot C.

transcription.tex: The other support exerts no force at the tipping point. Take moments about \(C\) to eliminate its unknown reaction. The beam’s midpoint is \(8-5=3\) m to the right of \(C\).\[mg(5)=45g(3),\qquad 5m=135.\]Woody’s mass is \(27\,\mathrm{kg}\).

transcription.tex: A non-uniform rod \(AB\), of length 10 m and weight 40 N, is suspended from a pair of light cables attached to \(C\) and \(D\) where \(AC=3\) m and \(BD=2\) m.\par When a weight of 25 N is hung from \(A\) the rod is on the point of rotating.\par Find the distance of the centre of mass of the rod from \(A\).

shapes.alt: Free-body diagram at the threshold of rotation about C. The plank weight acts at G.

transcription.tex: The rod is about to rotate about \(C\), so the cable at \(D\) is just slack and \(T_D=0\). Put \(AG=x\). Then the lever arm of the rod’s weight is \(x-3\).\par Take moments about \(C\) to eliminate \(T_C\).\[25(3)=40(x-3)\]\[75=40x-120,\qquad 40x=195.\]The centre of mass is \(4.875\,\mathrm m\) from \(A\).

transcription.tex: A beam AB has length 15 m. The beam rests horizontally in equilibrium on two smooth supports at the points P and Q, where AP = 2 m and QB = 3 m. When a child of mass 50 kg stands on the beam at A, the beam remains in equilibrium and is on the point of tilting about P. When the same child of mass 50 kg stands on the beam at B, the beam remains in equilibrium and is on the point of tilting about Q. The child is modelled as a particle and the beam is modelled as a non-uniform rod.\par (a) (i) Find the mass of the beam. (ii) Find the distance of the centre of mass of the beam from A.\par When the child stands at the point X on the beam, it remains horizontal and in equilibrium. Given that the reactions at the two supports are equal in magnitude,\par (b) find AX.

shapes.alt: The beam supports P and Q are two metres from A and three metres from B.

transcription.tex: Vertical equilibrium gives \(2R=75g\), so \(R=37.5g\). Take moments about \(A\): \(R(2+12)=25g(6)+50g(AX)\). Hence \(AX=(525-150)/50=7.5\) m.

Let the mass be \(M\) kg and its centre of mass be \(x\) metres from \(A\). At the first threshold, take moments about \(P\): \(M(x-2)=50(2)=100\). At the second, take moments about \(Q\): \(M(12-x)=50(3)=150\).\par Adding gives \(10M=250\), so \(M=25\) kg.

transcription.tex: Question 6

A non-uniform beam PQ, of mass m and length $8a$, hangs horizontally in equilibrium from two wires at M and N, where PM = a and QN = 2a, as shown in the diagram. The centre of mass of the beam is at the point O. A particle of mass $\tfrac34 m$ is placed on the beam at Q and the beam is on the point of tipping about N.\par (a) Show that $ON=\tfrac32a$.\par The particle is removed and replaced at the midpoint of the beam and the beam remains in equilibrium.\par (b) Find the magnitude of the tension in the wire attached at point $N$ in terms of $m$.

shapes.alt: Suspension wires at M and N and weight at O. The added particle is at Q in (a) and at the midpoint in (b).

transcription.tex: (a) At tipping, \(T_M=0\). Moments about \(N\):\[mg(ON)=\tfrac34mg(2a).\]\[ON=\tfrac32a.\]
(b) \(PO=6a-1.5a=4.5a\). Moments about \(M\) after moving the particle:\[T_N(5a)=mg(3.5a)+\tfrac34mg(3a).\]\[T_N=\frac{23}{20}mg.\]

transcription.tex: Question 7

A uniform beam AB, of weight W and length 14 m, hangs in equilibrium in a horizontal position from two vertical cables attached at points C and D where AC = 4 m and $BD=6$ m. A weight of 180 N is hung from A and the beam is about to tilt. The weight is removed and a different weight, V, is hung from B and the beam does not tilt. Find the maximum value of $V$.

shapes.alt: A fourteen-metre uniform beam with wires at C and D; the additional loads act at opposite ends in the two cases.

transcription.tex: First, \(T_D=0\). Moments about \(C\):\[180(4)=3W\quad\Rightarrow\quad W=240\text{ N}.\] At maximum \(V\), \(T_C=0\). About \(D\):\[240(1)=6V\quad\Rightarrow\quad V=40\text{ N}.\]
